images.after: What schema markup can and can't do
images.title: What schema markup does
images.alt: Comparison of what schema markup can do, such as label page content and make it eligible for rich results, and what it can't, such as raise rankings.
images.caption: Valid markup makes a page a candidate. Google still decides what to show.

columns.label: Can
points: State what a name, date or number means
Make a page eligible for rich results

columns.label: Can't
points: Raise your rankings on its own
Force a rich result to appear

images.title: Before you add rating markup
images.alt: Checklist of Google's star rating rules: eligible content types only, no self-serving reviews, real visible user ratings, and no fake reviews.
images.caption: If your site has no working review system, leave rating markup alone.

items: The page is about an eligible type, such as a product or recipe
It isn't an ordinary blog post
The reviews aren't about your own business
Visitors can see the ratings on the marked-up page
No ratings pulled in from other websites
Nothing made up: fake reviews can bring a manual action

images.title: Testing your markup
images.alt: Four steps to test schema: run the Rich Results Test, fix errors before warnings, use URL Inspection after publishing, then watch rich result reports.
images.caption: A passing test means the markup is valid, not that a rich result will appear.

items.title: Run the Rich Results Test
items.text: Paste the URL or code to see eligible types, errors and warnings

items.title: Fix errors first
items.text: A missing required property makes the item ineligible; then fix warnings

items.title: Inspect the live URL
items.text: Use URL Inspection in Search Console to confirm Google found it

items.title: Watch the reports
items.text: Check rich result reports for valid and invalid items over the next weeks
